title: Gwote Acha
localName: Gwote acha — gote, fonio, hungry rice
author: Abidemi Olayiwola
desc: Half a cup of fonio into three cups of broth with vegetables — five minutes and it is done, because acha cooks faster than any other grain in Nigeria.
longDesc: Acha is fonio, the ancient West African grain of the Jos Plateau, and the one thing everyone agrees on is that it cooks fast. This savoury porridge builds a broth with smoked meat, onion, garlic, bay and thyme, adds peppers and cabbage, then stirs in half a cup of fonio for about five minutes and finishes with spring onion and spinach. The author is open that she adapted the Plateau original to what she could buy — smoked turkey for biscuit bones, bouillon for dawadawa and dried prawns — so this is a documented adaptation rather than a traditional gwote.
steps: Heat the oil and soften the onion and garlic.
Add the bay leaves, thyme and smoked turkey, and build a broth — about 15 minutes.
Add the ground pepper, the red and green peppers and the cabbage, and cook about 10 minutes.
Rinse the acha and stir it in with the broth.
Leave to cook around 5 minutes. If the porridge becomes too thick, add some water to get your preferred consistency.
Stir in the spring onions and the spinach.
Taste, adjust the salt, and serve.
chefTips: Five minutes. Acha cooks faster than any other grain in Nigerian cooking and it will turn to paste if you treat it like rice.
Half a cup of acha to three cups of liquid gives a porridge. That is the only acha ratio published by any named source, and it is a porridge ratio rather than a swallow ratio.
Rinse the acha before it goes in. The grain is tiny and carries dust.
Add water at the end if it tightens. The author says so directly, and acha keeps absorbing after the heat is off.

A peer-reviewed study puts the optimum cooking time at 7.5 minutes at 100°C, judged on moisture uptake and thermal properties. That is slightly longer than this recipe's five and it is the most rigorous figure available.

This is a declared adaptation. Smoked turkey replaces biscuit bones and bouillon replaces dawadawa and dried prawns — the author says so — and the bay leaves and thyme are not traditional Plateau seasonings.
Acha is fonio, also called hungry rice, and it is one of the oldest cultivated grains in West Africa.
commonMistakes: Cooking it like rice, for twenty minutes.
Letting it tighten without adding water.
Expecting a traditional Plateau flavour from a dish seasoned with bay and thyme.
servedWith: On its own, as a porridge
sources: Adapted from 'Savoury Fonio Porridge', byline Abi Olayiwola, eatwellabi.com. Local name as printed: Gwote acha, 'from Plateau state, Nigeria'. Servings as printed: 4. Headnote as printed: 'A delicious savoury fonio porridge recipe inspired by gwote acha from Plateau state in Nigeria.'

Quantities exactly as printed: 2 tablespoons oil; 1 medium onion; 2 cloves garlic; 3 small bay leaves; 1 tablespoon thyme; 4 medium pieces smoked turkey; 1 teaspoon ground pepper; 1 red pepper; 1 green pepper; 1/2 small cabbage; salt to taste; 1/2 cup fonio; 3 spring onions; 1 cup spinach. FONIO : WATER = 1/2 cup : 3 cups.

Total time as printed: 35 minutes — 15 minutes meat and broth, 10 minutes vegetables, 5+ minutes fonio. DONENESS CUE as printed: 'Leave to cook for around 5 mins. If the porridge becomes too thick, you can add some water to get your preferred consistency.'

AUTHOR-FLAGGED DEVIATION, and it is substantial: she explicitly states she 'adapted the local recipe to use the ingredients available to me' and SUBSTITUTED SMOKED TURKEY FOR TRADITIONAL BISCUIT BONES, and BOUILLON FOR DAWADAWA AND DRIED PRAWNS. Her bay leaves and thyme are not traditional Plateau seasonings either. This is therefore an adaptation with a useful ratio rather than the traditional dish, and it is published as such.

THE ONE RIGOROUS COOKING TIME, from a peer-reviewed source: Raji, A.O., Nassam, H.O., Aruna, T.E., Raji, M.O., & Sani, M. (2017), 'Effect of cooking time on the physical, chemical and thermal properties of acha seeds', International Journal of Food Studies, 6(2), 178–191, DOI 10.7455/ijfs/6.2.2017.a5. Verbatim: 'Cooking times (2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 minutes) at 100°C were used', and the conclusion, 'Cooking for 7.5 minutes was appropriate using the moisture uptakes and thermal properties as criteria.' CRITICALLY: the WATER-TO-GRAIN RATIO IS NOT SPECIFIED in that paper — it does not state the seed-to-water proportion used in its trials.

SO THE STATE OF THE RECORD ON ACHA IS: cooking time can be published with confidence at 7.5 minutes at 100°C from a peer-reviewed source; the WATER RATIO IS UNDOCUMENTED in every source including the paper, and the half-cup-to-three-cups above is a porridge ratio from one adapted recipe rather than a general figure. Blog times disagree with the paper and with each other — 2 to 3 minutes, 5 minutes, against the 7.5-minute optimum.

GAPS, both specifically sought and both empty: TUWON ACHA, acha as a swallow, returned NOTHING from any named source. KUNUN ACHA, acha as a drink, returned NOTHING. So acha porridge is documented three times over while acha as a swallow and as a drink are not documented at all. Neither is published here.
No Berom-specific dish beyond acha was documented at all; searches surfaced only ethnographic pages about the Berom people rather than food.
reheating: Low heat with plenty of water — it thickens hard when cold.
healthBenefits: Fonio is gluten-free and unusually rich in the amino acids methionine and cysteine.
Very low glycaemic index, which is why it is recommended for diabetic diets.
High in fibre, iron and magnesium.
Cooks in minutes, which preserves more of its nutrients.
culturalNote: Acha is one of the oldest cultivated grains in West Africa and the Jos Plateau is its Nigerian home. It is called hungry rice in English, which is unkind to a grain with a better amino acid profile than most cereals — the name comes from its reliability in lean seasons rather than from any deficiency. It is badly under-documented, and anything written down about it is worth having.
